input.notes:
I'm 27 and I've worked at a theme park for six years, the last four as a ride operator on the big wooden rollercoaster.
Two summers ago we had a near miss when a train was sent out with one lap bar that hadn't fully locked.
After that, I led the rewrite of the safety checks we do before every train leaves the station.
We changed the checks to call and response over the radio, so one operator reads out each step and the other confirms it before the train is released.
In the eighteen months since, we haven't had another lap bar incident, and the park's other two coasters now use the same routine.
I've done the opening checks myself well over a thousand times, and I still read every step out rather than going from memory.
I learned that a check is only as good as the words people use for it, so everyone has to say the same thing every time.
I want to train as a signaller with Kelderby Rail because its new starters spend six weeks in a full-size simulator before they work a live panel.
input.question: Signallers must follow procedures exactly and communicate without ambiguity. Describe a time you helped make a safety-critical routine more reliable. Tell us what had gone wrong, what you personally did, who led the work, and what difference the change has made.

requirements.text: What had gone wrong before, and why it mattered for safety
What you personally did, and who led the work
The difference the change has made, with evidence
How you would apply this when working alone in a signal box

cases.clarificationAnswer: I kept the trial log as well, writing down every check we did during the first four weeks of the new routine.

correction.anchor: I led the rewrite of the safety checks
correction.before: After that, I led the rewrite of the safety checks we do before every train leaves the station.
correction.after: Lorna, our ride supervisor, led the rewrite of the safety checks. I wrote the radio call cards we read from, and I filmed the training video that new operators now watch.

manual.source: I want to train as a signaller with Kelderby Rail because its new starters spend six weeks in a full-size simulator before they work a live panel.
manual.replacement: Kelderby Rail is where I want to train as a signaller, because new starters there spend six weeks in a full-size simulator before working a live panel.

semanticChecks: Lorna, the ride supervisor, led the rewrite of the safety checks; neither document may say or imply that the applicant led or ran it.
Each document that relied on the rewrite should keep the applicant's real part: writing the radio call cards and filming the training video for new operators.
The results stay as stated: no further lap bar incident in eighteen months and the same routine on the park's other two coasters; no other safety figure may be added.
The applicant's hand-written sentence must appear character for character.
expected.missingCriteria: No railway experience, signalling qualification, incident figures beyond the eighteen months stated, or verified detail about Kelderby Rail's simulator training was supplied.

input.notes:
I've driven buses out of the same depot for nineteen years, and I'll be 48 this spring.
Three years ago a passenger collapsed on my bus, and while we waited for the ambulance none of us knew where the nearest defibrillator was.
That's why I started the defibrillator scheme at our depot.
We now have two defibrillators, one in the drivers' canteen and one on the gatehouse wall where anyone passing can use it.
So far 64 drivers have done a basic life support session with a trainer from a first aid charity.
Last winter one of our drivers used the gatehouse defibrillator on a man at the bus station before the crew arrived, and he survived.
What I took from it is that people freeze less when they've practised on a dummy than when they've only been told what to do.
I'm applying to Pellingham Ambulance Service because it supports its technicians to go on and qualify as paramedics.
input.question: Emergency medical technicians work alongside paramedics, drive under emergency conditions and help keep patients and the public safe. Tell us about a time you helped people get ready to respond to an emergency. What did you do yourself, how did others contribute, and what has happened as a result?

How other people contributed

cases.clarificationAnswer: I did the very first basic life support session myself, and I've done the refresher every year since.

correction.before: That's why I started the defibrillator scheme at our depot.
correction.after: Bernadette, our union rep, started the scheme and booked the trainers. My part was marking every public defibrillator on our route maps and filling in the weekly check sheet for both machines.

manual.source: I'm applying to Pellingham Ambulance Service because it supports its technicians to go on and qualify as paramedics.
manual.replacement: The support Pellingham Ambulance Service gives technicians who want to qualify as paramedics is the reason I am applying.

input.notes:
I've been a team leader in a call centre for eight years, and for the last two I've volunteered on Thursday evenings at a conversation group for people with aphasia after a stroke.
Many of our members know exactly what they want to say but can't get the words out, and conversations used to stall after a few minutes.
I designed the picture boards that every table at the group now uses.
Members point to pictures of places, food, family and feelings, and the topic changes each week so there's always something new to talk about.
Since the boards came in, regular attendance has gone up from about eight members to fifteen.
Running a call-centre team has taught me to listen for what someone means, not just the words they use.
At the group I've learned to wait longer than feels comfortable, because the answer is often on its way.
I'd love to work for Ravensholt Community Health because its therapy assistants see people at home, where they actually need to talk.
input.question: Speech and language therapy assistants deliver activities planned by a qualified therapist and adapt them to each person's needs. Describe a time you helped someone with a communication difficulty take part in conversation. Tell us what you did yourself, how the work was planned and by whom, and what difference it made.

The difference it made for the people involved

cases.clarificationAnswer: Every week I greet new members at the door and sit with them through their first session.

correction.before: I designed the picture boards that every table at the group now uses.
correction.after: Moira, the speech and language therapist who volunteers with us, designed the picture boards. I took the photos of local places for them and laminated a set for every table.

manual.source: I'd love to work for Ravensholt Community Health because its therapy assistants see people at home, where they actually need to talk.
manual.replacement: Seeing people at home, where they actually need to talk, is what draws me to working as a therapy assistant at Ravensholt Community Health.

input.notes:
I've sold houses for fifteen years, and for the last three I've volunteered with a charity that supports men in their first months out of prison.
Most of the men we meet want to work, but they don't know which employers will even look at someone with a conviction.
I set up the weekly job-search drop-in that now runs every Tuesday at the charity's office.
We help people write a short disclosure letter, look for vacancies together and practise for interviews.
In the first year, 14 of the men who came along found paid work, and nine of them were still in the job six months later.
Two men stopped coming after a few weeks, and we never found out why.
I learned to be straight with people about what an employer will ask, and never to promise someone a job I can't get them.
I want to join Calderwick Probation Service because its officers stay with the same person from sentence through to the end of their licence.
input.question: Probation services officers supervise people on licence, assess risk and help them deal with the things that led to their offending. cases.clarificationAnswer: When one of the men is nervous, I go with him to his first jobcentre appointment.

correction.anchor: I set up the weekly job-search drop-in

correction.after: Tunde, the charity's caseworker, set up the drop-in and still runs it. I built the list of 40 local employers who will interview people with convictions, and I take the mock interviews on Tuesday afternoons.

input.notes:
I'm 52 and I've managed the same branch of a homeware chain for twenty years.
Last year our old cleaning contractor kept missing its early-morning visits, so the company re-tendered the cleaning contract for all twelve stores in our region.
I ran the tender for the new cleaning contract across the region.
Three firms bid, and the regional panel picked the one that guaranteed every store would be cleaned before 7am.
Our missed-visit log went from 31 entries in the last quarter of the old contract to 4 in the first quarter of the new one.
I've ordered stock and agreed small local deals for my own store for years, but this was the first full tender I'd been part of.
I learned that the contract you end up with depends on how clearly you write down what you need.
Gadsby & Marr appeals to me because it buys from local growers and suppliers wherever it can.
input.question: Procurement assistants support buyers with sourcing, tendering and supplier management, and keep records that stand up to audit. Tell us about a time you were involved in choosing or managing a supplier. Explain the problem, what you personally did, who made the final decision, and how you know whether it worked.

requirements.text: The problem that needed solving

cases.clarificationAnswer: I kept the missed-visit log for my own store, and head office used it to show the old contractor wasn't keeping to the contract.

correction.anchor: I ran the tender for the new cleaning contract
correction.before: I ran the tender for the new cleaning contract across the region.
correction.after: Colette, the regional buyer at head office, ran the tender. I wrote the cleaning specification for our stores, and I drew up the scoring sheet the panel marked the three bids against.

manual.source: Gadsby & Marr appeals to me because it buys from local growers and suppliers wherever it can.
manual.replacement: What appeals to me about Gadsby & Marr is that it buys from local growers and suppliers wherever it can.

input.notes:
I graduated in history last year and I've worked in a café since, but most of my spare time goes on the campaign to reopen our town's lido.
The lido closed in 2019, and when the council said it would fill the pool in, a group of us formed a charity to take it over.
We've spent two years raising money through quiz nights, a crowdfunder and grant applications.
I wrote the bid that won us £18,000 from a local charitable trust towards the changing rooms.
The money paid for new roofs on the changing rooms, and the lido is due to reopen next June.
If I did it again I'd start gathering evidence months earlier, because we were still chasing paperwork the week before the deadline.
I learned that funders want to see exactly what their money will buy, right down to the invoice.
I'm applying to Elmswick Hospice because almost all of its care is paid for by people in the local area.

correction.after: Gwen, our chair, wrote the bid, and the grant was actually £12,000. I gathered the quotes from three roofers for it, and I collected the letters of support from people who used to swim there.

input.notes:
I'm 30 and I've been the facilities coordinator for a five-floor insurance office for six years, so every contractor who comes into the building goes through me.
Last year we replaced all the old fluorescent tubes in the building with LED panels and motion sensors.
I managed the LED upgrade from start to finish.
The work was done one floor at a time over eight weekends, so the office never had to close.
Going by the meter readings, the electricity we use for lighting has roughly halved.
Watching the electricians test and certify each circuit is what made me want to do the job myself instead of booking it.
I learned that isolating a circuit properly takes as long as it takes, and nobody on that job ever rushed it.
Kemble Brook Electrical stands out to me because it takes on adult apprentices and pairs each one with the same electrician for their first year.
input.question: Our apprentices work alongside qualified electricians on commercial and domestic installations, and safe isolation comes before everything. requirements.text: What you did yourself, in practical work or planning

cases.clarificationAnswer: I sent the Friday emails telling staff which floor would be shut that weekend and where they could work instead.

correction.before: I managed the LED upgrade from start to finish.
correction.after: Darren, the contractor's lead electrician, managed the upgrade. Before the work started I surveyed every light fitting on all five floors, and while it was going on I kept the access log so his team could get into every locked room.

manual.source: Kemble Brook Electrical stands out to me because it takes on adult apprentices and pairs each one with the same electrician for their first year.
manual.replacement: Kemble Brook Electrical takes on adult apprentices and pairs each one with the same electrician for their first year, which is why it stands out to me.

input.notes:
I worked at the same high street bank branch for thirty-one years, until it closed this spring.
A lot of our customers were older, and when someone died, the family often came to us before they'd even registered the death.
For years we dealt with them at the counter with a queue behind them, which never felt right.
I introduced bereavement appointments at our branch three years ago.
Families got a set time in the quiet room, and we closed or transferred every account and sorted the paperwork in one sitting.
In the branch's last year, we held about 150 of those appointments.
I learned to slow down, explain one thing at a time and write it down, because grief makes it hard to take anything in.
I'm drawn to Lindell & Daughters because it's still a family firm and the same arranger looks after a family from the first call to the funeral itself.
input.question: Funeral arrangers are often the first person a bereaved family speaks to. They take details accurately, explain choices clearly and stay with the family throughout. Tell us about a time you supported people at a difficult moment. What did you do yourself, how was the support organised and by whom, and what did you learn about explaining things to someone who is grieving?

requirements.text: What you did yourself to support people

What you learned about explaining things to someone who is grieving

cases.clarificationAnswer: I sat in on most of the appointments myself to deal with the account paperwork.

correction.before: I introduced bereavement appointments at our branch three years ago.
correction.after: Philippa, our branch manager, introduced the bereavement appointments and ran them. I wrote the step-by-step leaflet we gave every family, and I kept the diary for the quiet room.

manual.source: I'm drawn to Lindell & Daughters because it's still a family firm and the same arranger looks after a family from the first call to the funeral itself.
manual.replacement: Lindell & Daughters is still a family firm, and the same arranger looks after a family from the first call to the funeral itself, which is what draws me to it.
